facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; North Carolina ratified the U.S. Constitution on November 21, 1789, the 12th state to do so.
facts.nickname: The Tar Heel State (also called the Old North State); both are traditional nicknames that were never made official by law
facts.motto: Esse quam videri ("To be, rather than to seem"), adopted 1893
facts.name_origin: King Charles II of England named the colony Carolina to honor his father, King Charles I. "Carolus" is the Latin form of Charles.

government.legislature: North Carolina General Assembly (it first met in Raleigh in 1794 to 1795)
government.chambers: North Carolina Senate (50 senators) and North Carolina House of Representatives (120 representatives); members of both serve 2-year terms
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; the state constitution says no one may be elected governor for more than two terms in a row). The lieutenant governor has the same two-terms-in-a-row limit.
government.courts: Supreme Court of North Carolina (a Chief Justice and six Associate Justices, 7 in all; the General Assembly may add up to two more). Justices are elected by voters to 8-year terms. The court first met on January 1, 1819.
government.local: 100 counties. The General Assembly sets county lines and decides what powers counties, cities, and towns have, and voters in each county elect a sheriff to a 4-year term.
government.constitution: North Carolina has had three constitutions: 1776 (ratified December 18, 1776), 1868 (written during Reconstruction), and the current one, approved by voters on November 3, 1970, and known as the Constitution of 1971.
government.kid_line: "The people have a right to the privilege of education, and it is the duty of the State to guard and maintain that right." (Article I, Section 15)

long_ago.about: People have lived in what is now North Carolina for at least 10,000 years. Later, Mississippian culture communities lived here before the nations Europeans met.

The Cherokee speak an Iroquoian language. Their homelands included the Oconaluftee River valley in the west, where about 800 Cherokee avoided removal and where the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians lives today.

The Tuscarora, an Iroquoian-speaking nation, lived in eastern North Carolina. When settlers pushed onto their land and slave traders raided their towns, they fought the Tuscarora War (1711 to 1715); afterward many Tuscarora moved to New York and joined the Haudenosaunee as the Sixth Nation in 1722.

long_ago.nation: Algonquian-speaking coastal nations: Chowanoc, Roanoke, Pamlico, and Machapunga
long_ago.about: These nations spoke Algonquian languages. Roanoke Island, where the English tried to start a colony in the 1580s, carries the Roanoke people's name.
The Meherrin spoke an Iroquoian language, and the Catawba were another nation of the region. The Meherrin are still a state-recognized tribe in northeastern North Carolina today.

today.about: Federally recognized; headquartered in Cherokee, North Carolina, on the Qualla Boundary, land the tribe bought back that is held in trust and supervised by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (it is not a reservation).

Based in Robeson, Hoke, and Scotland Counties, with more than 68,000 members, the largest tribe east of the Mississippi River. North Carolina recognized the Lumbee in 1885; a 1956 federal law recognized the tribe but denied it the full benefits, and the Lumbee Fairness Act, signed December 18, 2025, gave the tribe full federal recognition as the 575th federally recognized tribe.
State-recognized tribe in Sampson and Harnett Counties.
State-recognized tribe in Halifax, Warren, and nearby counties.
State-recognized tribe in Hertford, Bertie, Northampton, and Gates Counties.

today.nation: Occaneechi Band of the Saponi Nation
today.about: State-recognized tribe in Orange and surrounding counties.
State-recognized tribe in Columbus and Bladen Counties.

first_peoples.today_note: The North Carolina Commission of Indian Affairs lists eight tribes recognized by the state. Two of them, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and the Lumbee Tribe (since December 2025), are also federally recognized. The state also works with four urban Indian associations in Cumberland, Guilford, Mecklenburg, and Wake Counties. North Carolina has the largest American Indian population of any state east of the Mississippi River.
sites: Museum of the Cherokee Indian and Oconaluftee Indian Village, on the Qualla Boundary in Cherokee
Great Smoky Mountains National Park, shared by North Carolina and Tennessee
Site of Fort Neoheroka in Greene County, the Tuscarora fort lost in 1713
Roanoke Island on the Outer Banks, home of the Roanoke people and site of the lost English colony of 1587

history.event: People are living in what is now North Carolina. Over time come Mississippian culture towns and the Cherokee, Tuscarora, Catawba, Meherrin, and coastal Algonquian nations.
Spanish captain Juan Pardo builds Fort San Juan at the Native town of Joara. In 1568 Native people drive out the Spanish soldiers and burn the forts.
English colonists settle on Roanoke Island, and Virginia Dare is born there. When John White returns in 1590, the colony has vanished.

The Tuscarora War. Settlers had taken Tuscarora land and slave traders had kidnapped Tuscarora people. In 1713, at Fort Neoheroka, about 950 Tuscarora are killed or captured, and many captives are sold into slavery.
Many Tuscarora who moved north join the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in New York as its Sixth Nation.
North Carolina adopts the Halifax Resolves, the first formal call by a colony for independence from Great Britain.
North Carolina ratifies the U.S. Constitution, becoming the 12th state.
George Moses Horton, an enslaved poet in Chatham County, publishes The Hope of Liberty, the first book by an African American published in the South.

Harriet Jacobs flees her enslaver in Edenton and hides for almost seven years in her free grandmother's attic before escaping north. The Treaty of New Echota gives away Cherokee homelands; most Cherokee are later forced west on the Trail of Tears, but about 800 Cherokee along the Oconaluftee River stay.
North Carolina secedes from the Union and joins the Confederacy in the Civil War.
Wilmington, the last Confederate port, falls to the Union. As Union troops arrive in 1865, enslaved people, including the poet George Moses Horton, are freed.
A new state constitution is written with Black delegates such as Abraham Galloway, who is then elected to the State Senate. North Carolina is restored to the Union in July 1868.
Henry Berry Lowry, leader of a Lumbee band that resisted the Confederate Home Guard and later fought the Ku Klux Klan, disappears after a raid on Lumberton and becomes a Lumbee folk hero.

trailblazers.name: Harriet Jacobs
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, author and freedom seeker
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Edenton, she fled her enslaver in 1835 and hid for almost seven years in the attic of her grandmother, a free Black woman, before escaping north. Her book Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861) told the truth about slavery, and during the Civil War she helped newly freed people.

trailblazers.name: George Moses Horton
trailblazers.text: While enslaved in Chatham County, he sold poems to University of North Carolina students in Chapel Hill, even before he had learned to write. In 1829 his book The Hope of Liberty made him the first African American to publish a book in the South. He was freed when Union troops arrived in 1865.

trailblazers.name: Abraham Galloway
trailblazers.group: Black American freedom seeker, soldier, and lawmaker
trailblazers.text: Born in Smithville (now Southport), he escaped slavery in 1857 by hiding in a ship bound for Philadelphia. In the Civil War he was a Union spy and recruited Black soldiers in New Bern, and in 1868 he helped write a new state constitution and was elected to the North Carolina Senate.

trailblazers.name: Henry Berry Lowry
trailblazers.text: In Robeson County during the Civil War, Lumbee people formed a band to avoid forced labor for the Confederacy, and in 1865 Lowry's father and brother were executed. Henry led the band, which later fought the Ku Klux Klan. He vanished in 1872 and became a folk hero to the Lumbee; others saw him as an outlaw.

trailblazers.name: Pauli Murray
trailblazers.group: Black American civil rights lawyer, writer, and priest
trailblazers.text: Raised in Durham by aunts, Murray finished first in the class at Howard University's law school. Murray's book States' Laws on Race and Color was called "the bible of the civil rights movement" by Thurgood Marshall. Murray helped found the National Organization for Women in 1966 and in 1977 became the first Black woman ordained an Episcopal priest.

trailblazers.name: Ella Baker
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: Born in Norfolk, Virginia, Ella Baker moved with her family to Littleton, North Carolina, when she was eight, and she graduated from Shaw University in Raleigh in 1927. She worked for the NAACP and helped set up the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. After the 1960 Greensboro sit-ins, she spoke at a youth conference at Shaw in April 1960, where the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was formed.

landforms: Appalachian Mountains in the west, including the Great Smoky Mountains
Mount Mitchell (about 6,684 feet), the highest point in the state
The Outer Banks, a chain of sandy barrier islands about 200 miles long
Cape Hatteras, called the "Graveyard of the Atlantic" for its many shipwrecks
geography.regions: North Carolina has three natural regions: the Atlantic Coastal Plain in the east, the Piedmont in the center, and the Appalachian Mountains in the west.

ecosystems.name: Longleaf pine savannas and bogs
ecosystems.about: Wet, open longleaf pine savannas on the Coastal Plain need frequent fire to stay open. They are home to the Venus flytrap, which grows naturally only within about 75 miles of Wilmington and traps insects to get nutrients that the sandy soil lacks.

ecosystems.name: Southern Appalachian forests (Great Smoky Mountains)
ecosystems.about: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, shared with Tennessee, has about 19,000 known species and is called the "Salamander Capital of the World," with up to 31 kinds of salamanders. It also has the only synchronous fireflies in America, which flash together in late May and early June.

ecosystems.name: Barrier islands and sounds (Outer Banks)
ecosystems.about: The Outer Banks drift several feet each year as wind and waves move sand. Wild horses, sometimes called banker ponies, live on Ocracoke Island, Shackleford Banks, and Currituck Banks.

science.weather: Hurricanes and tropical storms are the biggest hazards, along with flooding and tornadoes. Hurricane Hazel (1954) was the strongest storm to make landfall in the state, and Hurricane Helene was the most destructive storm of the 21st century there.
science.resources: Longleaf pine forests, farmland, rivers, and the coast. Tobacco, textiles, and furniture were once the big industries; today technology, medicines, banking, food processing, vehicle parts, and tourism lead the economy.
science.highlight: The Venus flytrap, North Carolina's state carnivorous plant (2005), grows wild only near Wilmington in the Carolinas. Its two-lobed trap shuts only when two trigger hairs are touched within seconds of each other, so raindrops do not fool it. Poaching flytraps has been a felony in North Carolina since 2014.

g3_ss.title: North Carolina's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map the three regions and Raleigh; meet the General Assembly (50 senators, 120 representatives), the governor, and the Supreme Court (7 justices); read Article I, Section 15 on the right to education.

g3_ss.title: North Carolina's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Cherokee, Tuscarora, and coastal Algonquian nations long ago, then the eight tribes recognized today, including the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and the Lumbee.

g3_ss.title: North Carolina Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies of Harriet Jacobs, George Moses Horton, Pauli Murray, and Ella Baker, with a timeline of where each lived.

g45_ss.title: North Carolina's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Cherokee, Tuscarora, Catawba, Meherrin, and Algonquian nations; the Tuscarora War (1711 to 1715) and the Sixth Nation of the Haudenosaunee; Cherokee removal and the people who stayed on the Oconaluftee.

g45_ss.title: Joara, Roanoke, and Colonial North Carolina
g45_ss.plan: Juan Pardo's Fort San Juan (1567), the Roanoke colony (1587), the Halifax Resolves (1776), and ratifying the Constitution as the 12th state (1789).

g45_ss.title: North Carolina 1789 to 1877
g45_ss.plan: Slavery and freedom seekers (Harriet Jacobs, Abraham Galloway), secession in 1861, the fall of Wilmington, the 1868 constitution, and the Lowry band in Lumbee country.

g3_sci.title: The Venus Flytrap
g3_sci.plan: How a plant can catch insects: trigger hairs, the two-touch rule, and why sandy bog soil makes it hungry for nutrients.

g3_sci.title: Hurricanes on the Coast
g3_sci.plan: What a hurricane is, Hurricane Hazel and Hurricane Helene, and how families prepare for storms and floods.

g3_sci.title: Salamanders and Fireflies of the Smokies
g3_sci.plan: Meet the red-cheeked salamander, which lives only in the Smokies, and the synchronous fireflies that flash together.

g45_sci.title: Fire and the Longleaf Pine
g45_sci.plan: Why longleaf pine savannas need fire, how much has been lost (about 3% of the old range remains), and what lives there.

g45_sci.title: Moving Islands: The Outer Banks
g45_sci.plan: Barrier islands, wind and waves, and why the Outer Banks shift several feet a year; shipwrecks at Cape Hatteras.

g45_sci.title: From Mountains to Sea
g45_sci.plan: Compare the three regions: elevation from Mount Mitchell to the coast, river basins that drain to the sounds, and the living things in each.
